questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a defensible denominator for a density calculation
questions.stem: A clinic note asks which denominator makes sense for describing how crowded a district is.

options.text: The area of land people can actually live and work on, rather than all of it.
The total population of the world, so that every district is measured the same way.
options.misconception: thinks a world total suits a local density

options.text: The number of houses in the district, since households are what people occupy.
options.misconception: substitutes a housing count for an area measurement

options.text: The area of the largest neighbouring district, which sets a fair comparison.
options.misconception: invents a neighbouring district as the comparison base

questions.explanation: Density is only as useful as its denominator, and counting unusable land flatters the district. Choosing habitable land answers the question a clinic asks about pressure on services.
questions.hint: Ask which land people can really use.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the density of a clustered core area
questions.stem: The district summary compares an average with a pattern: 2,000,000 people live in a county of 10,000 square kilometres, and 1,800,000 of them crowd into the 1,000 square kilometres of the central urban area. Using the urban figures only, what is the density of that area in people per square kilometre?
questions.explanation: The core holds 1,800,000 people in 1,000 square kilometres, so its density is 1,800 per square kilometre against a county average of 200. An average hiding the core tells a clinic little.
questions.hint: Divide the urban population by the urban area.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret two regions using arable land per person
questions.stem: A teaching file shows two ways of describing crowding: region A has 90,000 hectares of arable land and 1,800,000 people, while region B has 40,000 hectares and 400,000 people. Which statement about the two regions is correct?

options.text: Region A has the greater land pressure because its population is larger.
options.misconception: judges land pressure by the size of the population alone

options.text: Region A has more land per person, so its land pressure is lower than B's.
Region B has the greater land pressure because it has fewer hectares of arable land.
options.misconception: judges land pressure by the size of the arable area alone

options.text: The two regions have the same land pressure, since their ratios are close to each other.
options.misconception: assumes the two ratios are close when they differ sharply

questions.explanation: Region A works out at 20 hectares per 100 people and region B at 10, so B carries the tighter ratio of people to cultivable land. Land pressure is a ratio, and one half alone tells you nothing.
questions.hint: Work out hectares per person for each.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What the crude birth rate measures
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the crude birth rate counts and omits
questions.stem: The health board briefing explains what a birth rate counts and what it leaves out.

answer.exemplar: The crude birth rate counts live births in a year divided by the mid-year population, expressed per thousand people, so it covers the whole population in the denominator rather than only women of childbearing age. Because the denominator includes everyone, the rate reflects the age structure of a population as well as its fertility, which is why it is called crude and why two countries with the same rate need not be alike.

questions.explanation: The rate divides a year's live births by the whole mid-year population, so age structure enters the calculation along with fertility. That is why the measure is called crude.
questions.hint: Ask what stands in the denominator.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What the crude death rate measures
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limits of a crude death rate

stimulus.body: District hospital returns for the calendar year show 9,000 deaths in a mid-year population of 600,000. No age breakdown of the deaths is available, and the district also contains a large retirement community.

questions.stem: A patient's record quotes a hospital's annual figures and asks what the resulting death rate does and does not show.

options.text: That the district's mortality is high because its residents are mostly retired.
options.misconception: reads the rate as a measure of risk in old age

options.text: That the rate measures the risk of dying in each age group separately.
options.misconception: mistakes a crude rate for an age-specific rate

options.text: That it is a whole-population average that cannot separate age from cause.
That the death rate can be compared directly with a young district's rate.
options.misconception: assumes crude rates are comparable across age structures

questions.explanation: Dividing 9,000 deaths by 600,000 people gives 15 per thousand, but that average mixes the deaths of infants, adults and the very old. Without an age breakdown it is not a risk for any group.
questions.hint: Ask what the denominator does to the comparison.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate and identify the infant mortality rate
questions.stem: A district clinic works through a calculation in two steps: in one year there were 480 deaths among infants under one year and 20,000 live births in the same district. First convert the deaths to a rate per thousand live births, then state what that rate is called.

options.text: 24 per thousand live births, and it is called the crude death rate.
options.misconception: gets the denominator right but names the wrong indicator

options.text: 4 per thousand live births, and it is called the infant mortality rate.
options.misconception: divides by a thousand times too many births

options.text: 24 per thousand population, and it is called the infant mortality rate.
options.misconception: uses total population instead of live births

options.text: 24 per thousand live births, and it is called the infant mortality rate.

questions.explanation: 480 divided by 20,000 gives 24 per thousand live births, and infant deaths per thousand live births is the infant mortality rate. Live births form the denominator.
questions.hint: Ask what the denominator counts.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Define natural increase and its exclusions
questions.stem: The clinic handbook asks what natural increase actually means.

options.text: The excess of births over deaths in a year, before any migration is counted.
The number of people added to a district by people moving in from elsewhere.
options.misconception: confuses natural increase with net migration

options.text: The rate at which the population of a country grows over a century.
options.misconception: reads natural increase as long-run population growth

options.text: The number of live births recorded in a year, with deaths subtracted.
options.misconception: mixes births with births minus deaths

questions.explanation: Natural increase is the gap between the crude birth rate and the crude death rate, so it counts only what happens inside a population and ignores arrivals and departures.
questions.hint: Ask what is deliberately left out.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a density using habitable land as the denominator
questions.stem: A rural practice record lists two possible denominators: a region has 36,000,000 people and 240,000 square kilometres of land in total, but only 30,000 square kilometres is settled and workable. Using the settled land only, what is the density in people per square kilometre?
questions.explanation: Dividing 36,000,000 people by the 30,000 square kilometres of settled land gives 1,200 per square kilometre, against 150 for the whole region. The denominator changes the picture of pressure.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a contrast between regional and built-up density
questions.stem: The screening report interprets two densities for one county: its overall density is 30 people per square kilometre, but the density inside its one built-up district reaches 900 per square kilometre. What does this pair of figures tell a clinic?

options.text: That the county's services should be located in the empty rural interior.
options.misconception: reads the low average as a reason for rural services

options.text: That demand is concentrated in the built-up district, not spread across the county.
That the county's overall density figure has been calculated incorrectly.
options.misconception: supposes the mismatch between the two figures means an error

options.text: That the built-up district's population is likely to fall over the next decade.
options.misconception: reads the contrast as a forecast of decline

questions.explanation: Averages conceal concentration, and the contrast between 30 and 900 shows where people live and where clinics will be used. The county-wide figure is a poor guide to siting.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what arable land density measures and its uses
questions.stem: A community medicine note explains the ratio of arable land to population and what it is used for.

answer.exemplar: Arable land density measures how much cultivable land is available per person, usually expressed in hectares per person or as the number of people each hectare has to feed. It is used to judge whether a region's food system is under pressure, and to compare regions whose total sizes and population totals differ so much that raw totals would mislead. It says nothing directly about yields, trade or the quality of the land.

questions.explanation: The measure compares cultivable land with the number of people to feed, so it is a ratio rather than a total. It suits comparing regions of different sizes, but says nothing about yields.
questions.hint: Ask what a ratio of land to people can tell.

questions.topic: What the crude birth rate measures
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the crude birth rate and identify its denominator

stimulus.body: The district returns for one year record 12,000 live births in a mid-year population of 300,000. The same district records 4,500 deaths in that year, and 240 of the newborn babies died before their first birthday.

questions.stem: A hospital bulletin quotes a decade of mortality figures and asks what the district's birth rate amounts to.

options.text: 40 births per thousand, so the district's population is replacing itself.
options.misconception: interprets the rate as showing population replacement

options.text: 4 per thousand, since the births must be divided by the population in thousands.
options.misconception: divides by thousands twice instead of once

options.text: 40 births per thousand of the whole mid-year population.
80 births per thousand, since births should be compared with women of childbearing age.
options.misconception: insists the denominator must be the childbearing population

questions.explanation: 12,000 live births over a mid-year population of 300,000 gives 40 births per thousand. Because the denominator is everyone rather than women of childbearing age, the rate is crude.
questions.hint: Ask what the denominator is and how it is scaled.

questions.topic: What the crude death rate measures
questions.learningObjective: Compare two crude death rates and identify the higher
questions.stem: A clinic worksheet works through a two step comparison: a district recorded 6,000 deaths in a year and its mid-year population was 300,000, while a second district recorded 3,000 deaths with a mid-year population of 100,000. First express both death rates per thousand, then state which district has the higher rate.

options.text: Both districts have 20 per thousand, so the rates are identical.
options.misconception: reaches the right rates but draws the wrong conclusion

options.text: The first district is higher at 20 per thousand against 30 in the second.
options.misconception: swaps the two rates when comparing them

options.text: The second district is higher at 20 per thousand against 30 in the first.
options.misconception: assigns the higher rate to the wrong district

options.text: Both districts have 20 per thousand, so neither has a higher rate.

questions.explanation: 6,000 deaths over 300,000 people gives 20 per thousand, and 3,000 over 100,000 also gives 20 per thousand. Equal ratios mean equal crude rates, whatever the totals show.
questions.hint: Scale each ratio by a thousand before comparing.

questions.topic: What the crude death rate measures
questions.learningObjective: Define the crude death rate and its components
questions.stem: The practice manual defines the crude death rate carefully and asks what it divides.

options.text: Deaths in a year by the mid-year population, expressed per thousand.
Deaths in a year by the number of live births in the same year.
options.misconception: uses live births as the denominator for a death rate

options.text: Deaths of infants by the number of live births in the same year.
options.misconception: confuses the crude death rate with the infant mortality rate

options.text: Deaths in a year by the number of households in the district.
options.misconception: substitutes a household count for a population denominator

questions.explanation: The crude death rate takes all deaths in a year over the mid-year population and expresses the result per thousand people. Dividing deaths by births produces an infant rate instead.
questions.hint: Ask which numerator and denominator are used.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate natural increase from crude rates
questions.stem: A district report calculates natural change for a year: the crude birth rate was 28 per thousand and the crude death rate was 12 per thousand. What is the natural increase, in births minus deaths per thousand of population?
questions.explanation: Natural increase is the crude birth rate minus the crude death rate, so 28 minus 12 gives 16 per thousand, or 1.6 per cent a year before migration. It measures change from within the population.
questions.hint: Subtract the death rate from the birth rate.

questions.learningObjective: Compare two districts using arable land per person
questions.stem: The health survey reads two arable land measures: district X has 45,000 hectares of arable land for 900,000 people, while district Y has 60,000 hectares for 300,000 people. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: District X has more arable land in total, so it feeds its people more easily.
options.misconception: compares the districts by totals, not per person

options.text: District Y has more arable land per person, so its land pressure is lower.
District X has less arable land per person, so it faces the greater pressure.
options.misconception: reverses which district has the tighter ratio

options.text: The two districts have identical land pressure, since totals scale with population.
options.misconception: assumes per-capita figures follow automatically from totals

questions.explanation: District X has 50 hectares per 100 people and district Y has 200, so Y's land pressure is lower. Land pressure is a ratio, and raw totals hide the difference between districts of different sizes.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why density and distribution must be distinguished
questions.stem: A clinical audit explains why density and distribution have to be kept apart.

answer.exemplar: Density is a single average figure for a whole area, whereas distribution describes how people are arranged across that area, clustered in towns or spread evenly. A district of uniformly low density and a district with the same average but dense towns and empty countryside are completely different places to work in, and only the second description tells a service planner where demand sits. The two measures answer different questions and neither can substitute for the other.

questions.explanation: Density gives one average for an area; distribution shows how people are arranged across it. Two districts with the same average can be very different places to work in.
questions.hint: Ask what each measure can and cannot show.

options.text: The city district has no land pressure because it owns no farmland at all.
options.misconception: mistakes owning farmland for the absence of land pressure

options.text: The agricultural district has the worse position because it must feed 250,000 people.
options.misconception: judges the farming district by its own numbers alone

options.text: The city district depends on the agricultural district, so their positions are linked.
Both districts are equally secure because their combined totals balance out.
options.misconception: assumes the two districts balance each other out

questions.explanation: The agricultural district works out at 12 hectares per 100 people and the city has none of its own, so the city must draw on land outside its boundary. The two positions are linked.
questions.hint: Ask where the city's food actually comes from.

options.text: Both are 50 per thousand, so the districts are equal on this measure.
options.misconception: gives the same rate to both districts

options.text: District B is higher at 50 per thousand against 10 in district A.
options.misconception: swaps the rates when naming the higher district

options.text: District A is higher at 50 per thousand against 10 in district B.
options.misconception: reverses which district has the higher infant rate

options.text: District A is 50 per thousand and district B is 10, so A is higher.

questions.explanation: 300 over 6,000 live births gives 50 per thousand in district A, while 300 over 30,000 gives 10 in district B. Equal numbers of infant deaths can describe very different conditions.
questions.hint: Use live births as the denominator for both.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret natural increase alongside net migration
questions.stem: The population office interprets a county's vital rates: the crude birth rate is 22 per thousand, the crude death rate is 11 per thousand, and net migration is a loss of 3 per thousand. What does this tell you?

options.text: The county's population is growing because births exceed deaths by enough.
options.misconception: ignores the effect of net migration on the total change

options.text: Natural increase is 11 per thousand, but migration means the total change is smaller.
The county's population must be shrinking, because net migration is negative.
options.misconception: concludes decline from the migration figure alone

options.text: The death rate is unusually high, since it sits at half the birth rate.
options.misconception: judges the death rate without a comparison standard

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What the crude death rate measures
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limitation of the crude death rate
questions.stem: A health education note explains what the crude death rate leaves out.

answer.exemplar: The crude death rate counts every death in a year over the whole mid-year population and applies no adjustment, so the shape of the population's age structure works straight into the figure. A district with many older residents will show a higher rate than one with the same health services but a younger population, even though nothing about care has changed. That is why comparisons are usually made within a country over time, or after adjusting for age.

questions.explanation: Because no age adjustment is applied, the population's age structure pushes the crude rate up or down. Comparisons are therefore usually made within a country over time, or after age-standardising.
questions.hint: Ask what the figure takes no account of.

The first district's figures must have been recorded incorrectly somewhere.
options.misconception: supposes one district's figures are in error

questions.explanation: Equal crude rates do not mean equal circumstances, because the second district has many more older residents. Without age-adjustment, the comparison tells you little about the quality of care.
questions.hint: Ask what the age structure does to the comparison.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why natural increase differs from population growth
questions.stem: A teaching session explains why natural increase is not the same as population growth.

answer.exemplar: Natural increase compares the crude birth rate with the crude death rate and so measures only what happens to a population from within: births minus deaths. It ignores migration entirely, which can be the larger force in many districts, and a place can have a healthy surplus of births and still shrink if people leave faster than they are born. Population growth is the sum of natural increase and net migration, and only that sum describes what the numbers actually do.

questions.explanation: Natural increase counts only births minus deaths and ignores migration, which may be the larger force in a district. Total change is natural increase plus net migration.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be added to get total change.

options.text: The district's density should be reported as a household count rather than an area figure.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rate must state its denominator
questions.stem: A clinic leadership note explains why a rate needs a stated denominator.

answer.exemplar: Every demographic rate is a ratio, so the same numerator can be made to look large or small by changing what it is divided by. questions.topic: What the crude death rate measures
questions.learningObjective: Explain why crude rates are called crude
questions.stem: A clinical seminar explains why crude rates are called crude.

answer.exemplar: The word marks what the calculation does not do. A crude rate takes the whole population as its denominator and applies no adjustment for the age or sex structure of the people counted, so any unusual composition of the population passes straight into the result. A district of retired people will show a high crude death rate and a district of young families a low one, even where care is identical. The measures are useful and easy to calculate; they are simply blunt instruments.

questions.explanation: A crude rate uses the whole population and makes no adjustment for age or sex, so unusual composition passes straight into the result. The measures are useful and easy to calculate, but blunt.

questions.hint: Convert both to hectares per person.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain distribution and density with a service example
questions.stem: A primary care note explains the difference between distribution and density with a clinic example.

answer.exemplar: Density is one number for an entire area, while distribution describes the arrangement of people within it, and the difference matters because services are consumed where people live rather than where averages fall. A county can hold 200 people per square kilometre on average and still deliver almost all of its care in one town of 50,000 people, with the rest of the map empty. Density alone would suggest spreading clinics evenly, which is exactly the wrong conclusion.

questions.explanation: Density is one number for an area; distribution shows where people are within it, and services are used where people live. A county averaging 200 per square kilometre may serve one town.
questions.hint: Ask where the services are actually used.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Separate density findings from land pressure findings

stimulus.body: A field survey records that one district has 600,000 people, 12,000 square kilometres of land and 180,000 hectares of arable land. A second district has 300,000 people, 30,000 square kilometres of land and 90,000 hectares of arable land.

questions.stem: A field survey record quotes a district's population figures and asks what the two districts show.

options.text: The first district is denser at 50 per square kilometre against 10 in the second.
options.misconception: stops at the density comparison and ignores land pressure

options.text: The first district has 0.3 hectares per person and the second has 0.15, so the second is worse.
options.misconception: mis-scales the second district's land ratio

options.text: The first district has 0.3 hectares per person, the same as the second, but five times the density.
The first district is denser, and its greater population per hectare means less land pressure.
options.misconception: assumes higher density means lower land pressure

questions.explanation: Both districts have 0.3 hectares per person, so their land pressure matches, yet the first is five times denser at 50 per square kilometre against 10. Density and land pressure are separate findings.
questions.hint: Ask for both ratios before comparing.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Compare infant mortality across two districts
questions.stem: A health course compares infant mortality across two districts: district A has a crude birth rate of 36 per thousand and 360 infant deaths against 12,000 live births, while district B has a birth rate of 24 per thousand and 180 infant deaths against 18,000 live births. First work out each infant mortality rate, then say which is higher.

options.text: Both are 30 per thousand live births, so the districts are equal.
options.misconception: reports equal infant rates for two different districts

options.text: District A is 3 per thousand and district B is 10, so district B is higher.
options.misconception: mis-scales district A and misnames the higher one

options.text: District A is 30 per thousand and district B is 10, so district B is higher.
options.misconception: reverses which district has the higher infant mortality

options.text: District A is 30 per thousand and district B is 10, so district A is higher.

questions.explanation: 360 over 12,000 live births gives 30 per thousand in district A, and 180 over 18,000 gives 10 in district B. The crude birth rate is not needed, since live births form the denominator.
questions.hint: Use live births for both districts.
